newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Govt officials welcome Serbian privatisation law.
newsitem.headline: Govt officials welcome Serbian privatisation law.

text.p: Yugoslav government officials and economists welcomed on Monday the new Serbian privatisation law hoping it will help revive the capital-starved economy.
Yugoslav Deputy Prime Minister Danko Djunic said the law will live up to its task and stimulate other reforms.

"Privatisation is necessary but not sufficient. We must also rehabilitate banks, restructure the entire economy, adopt other laws, change the existing ones where necessary to create transparent climate for a market economy," he said.
Djunic said the law paid particular attention to interests of workers, pensioners, state employees, army officers, police.
"Privatisation cannot create funds overnight. But we can at least expect more transparent rules of the game," Djunic said.
Some analysts feared irregular and frequently delayed payment of wages and pensions could pose a big obstacle to the process, heavily reliant on sale of shares to employees and pensioners.
Serbia presented its new draft privatisation law refraining from mass privatisation but envisaging heavy discounts for employees, pensioners and other investors.
Privatisation will not be compulsory but legislators said the size of offered discounts will stimulate the process.
After one month of fine-tuning the draft, the final version will be submitted to the parliament with privatisation expected to begin early in July.

"This year has been rightfully announced as a reform year because reforms are an important precondition for the restructuring of the Serbian economy and its integration with international economy and finance," Serbian Prime Minister Mirko Marjanovic said.
"We see ownership transformation and privatisation as part of the entire reform process," he said.
Marjanovic said the law is based on efficiency, fairness and transparency and will be highly stimulating.
Serbian Privatisation Minister Milan Beko said the law changes the ownership structure of the Serbian economy and is the most important legal document of the state.
Beko promised the government will inform the public on the privatisation process via all media.
The law will be accompanied by other projects -- repayment of all hard-currency savings and rehabilitation of banks.
The first stage of privatisation will last three years.
Shares will be sold with discounts, within capitalisation issues or debt-for-equity swaps.
Privatisation receipts will be directed to three state funds: 50 percent to the Serbian development funds and 25 percent to the Pension fund and Labour market office each.

"The draft is a solid basis to digest all comments and prepare a final version aimed at reviving Serbia's economy," said Danilo Pantovic, secretary of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce and spokesman of the Yugoslav Left (JUL) party.
The National Bank of Yugoslavia Vice-Governor Ratko Banovic said he hoped for a soon implementation of the law.

"We expect positive results and to get a healthy banking sector, without which there is no revival of production. It is less important how many banks we have, but it is more important to create an efficient banking system," Banovic told Reuters.
Jurij Bajec of the Economics Institute and a member of the government economics team said the law aimed to make up for the lack of voucher privatisation.
"Our intention was to offer heavy incentives and eliminate the socially-owned capital," he told Reuters.
Bajec insisted privatisation was a process without return.
"Those who opened door to privatisation cannot step back and must finish the task."
"Privatisation will be transparent. Those controversial, big and heavily indebted companies will be privatised according to special governement programmes," he said.
The law should attract foreign investors for a simple reson that it exists, Bajec added. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
